analysis.one_liner: Caps national greenhouse gas emissions with an auction program, returning most revenue to households, workers, and polluted communities.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late July 2024 with zero cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to set a declining, enforceable national limit on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, refineries, fuel producers, and large industrial facilities, reaching net-zero by 2050. Companies would buy emission allowances at quarterly auctions with a rising price floor, and the revenue would be returned mostly to households: direct rebates for low-income consumers, state-run efficiency and ratepayer programs, a worker and community assistance fund for people hurt by the energy transition, and extra investment in communities with heavy local pollution. It also requires prevailing wages on projects it funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income households, through direct rebates funded by 15% of allowances auctioned each year and state consumer-protection programs; workers and communities dependent on fossil fuel jobs, through a dedicated Worker and Community Assistance Fund and a new federal transition office; and residents of heavily polluted neighborhoods, which would see local polluters charged double the allowance cost and receive a 10% share of auction proceeds for cleaner-air investments. States, tribes, and local governments also get funds for efficiency, clean energy, and climate resilience projects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, transition workers, and polluted communities

how_it_helps.text: Sets enforceable annual emission targets for covered entities: at least 5% below 2022-2024 levels by 2026, no more than 50% of 2005 levels by 2030, 30% by 2040, and 10% by 2050, with a national net-zero goal by 2050.

Auctions 15% of allowances each year specifically to fund direct rebates to low-income consumers, and gives states and tribes a declining share of allowances they must sell and use for consumer benefit — energy efficiency, low-emission fuel incentives, or direct ratepayer assistance.

Deposits proceeds from 5% of allowances into a Worker and Community Assistance Fund and creates a federal Office of Energy and Economic Transition to study and assist adversely affected workers and communities.

Requires sources located in designated 'Cleaner Air Communities' to surrender twice the allowances per ton emitted, and funds a Cleaner Air Community Fund with 10% of allowances, steering extra cleanup investment to overburdened neighborhoods.
Requires prevailing wages for laborers and mechanics on all projects funded by allowance proceeds, and applies the same standard to state and tribal programs.

Includes market guardrails: no bidder may buy more than 5% of allowances at any auction, winning bidders must be publicly disclosed, and the bill directs market oversight of the allowance trading system.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and importers, refineries, coal-fired and gas-fired power plants, natural gas utilities, and large industrial emitters (cement, steel, chemicals, aluminum), which would have to buy allowances for every ton they emit, with civil penalties of three times the auction price for noncompliance. Some of those costs would pass through to consumers in fuel and electricity prices before rebates arrive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and large industrial emitters

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would raise fuel and electricity prices across the economy, and those price increases would hit consumers before any rebate arrives — a real timing and distribution burden even if most revenue is returned to households.

Energy-intensive, trade-exposed industries like steel, cement, and chemicals would receive free output-based allowances — 15% of the cap in the first years, declining to zero over 30 years — which reduces auction revenue available for rebates and blunts their incentive to cut emissions.

Allowances would be freely tradable by anyone, creating a large financial market in pollution permits; the bill tries to contain this with purchase limits, ownership disclosure, and market oversight, but a trading market adds complexity and cost to a program that could otherwise be a simpler fee-and-rebate system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is unusually consumer-forward for a climate cap: most allowance value flows back to households, transition workers, and polluted communities rather than to industry, and it includes real labor standards and market guardrails. The honest costs are near-term energy price increases that land before rebates do, and heavy administrative complexity — the bill was referred to four separate committees at once, a sign of how sprawling it is. On the merits it weighs in favor of households, but with zero cosponsors in either party it was never going to move in a Republican-controlled House in the final months of a session.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in four House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Science, Space, and Technology — without a single hearing, markup, or floor vote from its July 2024 introduction until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Tonko introduced the bill on July 30, 2024, in the final months of the 118th Congress.

It was referred to four committees at once — Energy and Commerce, plus Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Science, Space, and Technology — a multi-committee referral that requires each to act before the bill can advance.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in the House, including among fellow Democrats.
The only further action was a routine subcommittee referral on December 17, 2024, two weeks before the session ended; no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without reaching either chamber's floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers, refineries, and other large emitters are better off because the bill died: they never faced allowance costs, a rising carbon price floor, or triple penalties for excess emissions. Households, transition workers, and polluted communities are worse off — the rebates, worker assistance, and cleaner-air investments it contained never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large emitters, spared the carbon cap

for.name: Rep. Paul Tonko
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor; no other member joined.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee (primary committee of referral)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it received no committee action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor or scheduled it for consideration at any point in the five months before the session ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split can be measured — but the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, including among the 216 House Democrats, signaling no organized support even within the sponsor's own caucus.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and coal producers and refiners
industries.note: They would pay for an allowance on every ton attributable to their fuels, with a price floor starting at $15 and rising 5% plus inflation annually, and triple penalties for noncompliance. Their avoidance of these costs is the main reason the bill's death benefits them. Costs would partly pass to consumers, but most revenue returns to households as rebates.

industries.industry: Fossil-fired electric utilities and natural gas distributors
industries.note: Power sources of 25 megawatts or more and large gas local distribution companies are covered entities that must surrender allowances for emissions and for gas their customers burn. State consumer programs funded by the bill partially offset bills, but the industry's direct compliance interest ran against the cap.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive trade-exposed manufacturers (steel, cement, chemicals, aluminum)
industries.note: They would bear allowance costs but receive free output-based allowances — 15% of the cap initially, tapering to zero over 30 years — designed to keep them competitive against foreign rivals. This cushions them substantially while slightly reducing revenue available for consumer rebates.

Allowances would be freely tradable by anyone, creating a new multi-billion-dollar commodity market with quarterly auctions. The bill tries to contain speculation with a 5% per-auction purchase limit, ownership disclosure, and market oversight provisions.

State and tribal grant programs, an Energy Innovation Fund, a Negative Emissions Activities Fund, and consumer electrification and efficiency rebates would channel auction proceeds into demand for clean power, storage, efficiency retrofits, and zero-emission vehicles.
